proxy_language: Proto-Yukaghir (reconstructed ancestor of Tundra and Kolyma Yukaghir), with Proto-Tungusic as a secondary areal reference
proxy_rationale: The Sumnagin culture (c. 8000-5000 BCE, Yakutia, Aldan-Lena region) is known only archaeologically. No linguistic identification is secure. Yukaghir is the most defensible proxy because it is a pre-Tungusic, pre-Turkic language family of northeastern Siberia whose speakers plausibly descend from Mesolithic and Neolithic populations of Yakutia, and Yukaghir-speaking territory once extended across the Lena-Kolyma region. The link is speculative: Sumnagin may equally have been ancestral to Yukaghir, Yeniseian, or an extinct language. Uralic-Yukaghiric ties (Nikolaeva 2006, Piispanen 2013) are debated. Proto-Yukaghir forms therefore serve as a plausible-sounding but unprovable model. Forms are based on Kolyma and Tundra Yukaghir, with reconstructions marked by asterisks.
phonology: Based on Kolyma/Tundra Yukaghir (Nikolaeva 2006). Vowels: i, e, a, o, u, plus central/front ö, ü and long vowels in the modern languages. Consonants: stops p, t, c (affricate [ts]/[tʃ]), k, plus palatal stop ť (c-hacek in some notations); voiced d, g and b in some positions; fricatives s, š (written š), ɣ (g with diacritic), h in loans; nasals m, n, ŋ (ng), ń; laterals l, ľ; rhotic r; glides j, w. Vowel harmony operates in Yukaghir (labial/palatal-type, ATR-like split) in some suffix alternations. Palatalization of coronals is phonemic. For game use, the inventory is simplified to a plain Latin set.
phonotactics: Syllable shapes (C)V(C); word-initial consonant clusters are absent; medial clusters are limited, typically nasal+stop (nd, ng, mp), r/l+C, or geminates. Word-final consonants are possible (n, l, r, k, t, m, ŋ) but vowel-final words are very common. Stress is not a major spelling factor. Native roots are typically one to three syllables. Avoid word-initial r- (rare in native Yukaghir roots; mostly loans) and word-initial ŋ.
orthography: Use plain Latin transliteration in the style of Nikolaeva/Maslova: a, e, i, o, u, ö, ü; p, t, k, c, s, š, h, m, n, ng for ŋ, l, r, j, w, d, g, b. Prefer ASCII where possible (š -> sh, ŋ -> ng); no apostrophes or hyphens inside a word; compounds are written as separate words or fused.
morphology: Yukaghir is agglutinative and suffixing, with a rich verbal system featuring focus marking. Nouns take case suffixes such as nominative -ø, accusative -ŋ/-nun, locative -gi/-ŋi, instrumental -le/-lek, genitive/possessive suffixes -ŋ ~ -k. Plural suffix is -pe (-pul in some dialects). Derivational suffixes include -lie (diminutive/qualitative), -ne/-ñe (nominalizer), -dü, -l (verbal nouns). Roots are monosyllabic or disyllabic CVC(V). Reduplication occurs in some expressive forms. There are no noun classes.
compounding: Compounds are head-final: modifier then head (determiner-noun). Genitive constructions place the possessor before the possessed with a genitive suffix or juxtaposition: 'X of Y' = Y(-gen) X. Agent nouns ('Y-maker') are built as object + verb root + nominalizer, e.g. object-verb-ne. Place names use locative or collective suffixes on a noun root.
noun_phrase_order: Modifier before head: adjective/noun modifier + noun; possessor + possessed; demonstrative + noun; numeral + noun. Head-final throughout.

worked_examples.name: luŋ kudene
worked_examples.gloss: luŋ 'stone' + kude- 'kill' + nominalizer -ne (object + verb + agent suffix)

sources: Nikolaeva, Irina. A Historical Dictionary of Yukaghir (Mouton de Gruyter, 2006)
Maslova, Elena. A Grammar of Kolyma Yukaghir (Mouton de Gruyter, 2003)
Maslova, Elena. A Grammar of Tundra Yukaghir (Mouton de Gruyter, 2003)
Piispanen, Peter. 'Uralic-Yukaghir lexical correspondences', Journal de la Societe Finno-Ougrienne (2013)
Mochanov, Yuri A. Sumnagin culture archaeological studies (Siberian Arctic archaeology, 1970s-1990s)
Glottolog entry for Yukaghir; ASJP wordlists for Yukaghir varieties
notes: The Sumnagin-Yukaghir link is a hypothesis with no direct evidence; treat all names as evocative, not authentic. Roots for kinship and landscape terms are approximate Kolyma/Tundra forms simplified for game use; exact vowel quality and diacritics may differ in Nikolaeva's notation. No word may be identical to a Modern Irish, Scottish Gaelic or Manx word, since Yukaghir is not Goidelic.
